name: Carla Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pick up parcels at nine from the depot behind the retail park, in my own little grey hatchback, and I do the villages out past the reservoir. It's usually 60 to 80 parcels, and I know which farm has the dog and which old lady wants it left in the coal shed. On Saturdays I do takeaway orders in town for extra. I like being out on my own, but the back seat full of boxes and the app timing me wear me down.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to this work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I worked in my mum's bakery on Church Street from fourteen, then she cut back her hours and I needed something. A girl from church said the parcel app paid weekly, so I signed up five years ago and never left. I live with my fiancé Tomasz, who drives a forklift at the supermarket warehouse, and we're getting married next August. I don't do any of the AI chat stuff, I only touch the app because I have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. That's what I'd want, to be honest. Leave things as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was a lot of noise from people in cities who sit at computers. At church coffee I'd probably say thank goodness. I don't post online much, maybe a photo of the reservoir now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means I keep worrying about the same things I worry about now. The app pays per block, and the blocks have got shorter since spring, so I'm earning less for the same miles. My car's got 140,000 miles on it, and if the gearbox goes before the wedding, I don't know what we'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my villages and my Saturdays, same as now. I'd put a bit more aside every week for the wedding and the car, maybe 30 more. I'd ask the depot manager if there are any longer blocks going, because I'd rather drive more than sit at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly. But the money's still tight, so it's not like everything's rosy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first if the car did break down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding flowers, probably, and maybe the second band my mum wants. We'd ask Tomasz's uncle, who does cars, to look at it before we paid a garage. Family first, that's how we've always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the blocks have got shorter. Who decides that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody you can talk to. There's a phone number that goes to a recording and a chat window that's a computer. I liked it better when Pete at the depot just told you what was going on.

say: I'd say AI was mostly **noise from cities** by people who sit at computers.
At church coffee I'd say **thank goodness** it stayed that way.
think: The app's **shorter blocks** already mean less money for the same miles.
My car has **140,000 miles** on it, and a breakdown before the wedding would hurt.
There's **nobody to talk to** at the app, only a recording.
do: Keep driving my **village route** and Saturday takeaways as now.
Save about **30 more a week** for the wedding and the car.
Ask the depot manager for **longer blocks**.
feel: Still **tight on money**, so not fully at ease.
S0.quote: My car's got 140,000 miles on it, and if the gearbox goes before the wedding, I don't know what we'd do.
fieldNote: Her pressures are **old-fashioned ones**: an old car, a wedding and shrinking app blocks.
She resents the app for having **no human voice**, more than any AI.
Her first fallback is always **family**, like Tomasz's uncle fixing the car.
Uneasy fits: work holds, but money is tight and the car is a risk.

steps.text: Keep the village parcel route and Saturday takeaway shifts
Save 30 more a week towards the wedding and the car

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's the office jobs that get it. I don't sit at a desk, so I suppose that's someone else's worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the depot I'd say, well, it's the office people's problem, parcels still need hands. At church I'd say I won't be using any of it, and my friends would nod. I'm not one of those who's on her phone asking a computer things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it creeps up on me through the app. They already plan the routes with a computer, and if it gets cleverer they'll squeeze more parcels into the same hours and pay us less. And Tomasz's warehouse is the sort of place that gets robots first, he's already seen the robot pallet movers at the other site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, but I'd stop the extra things, like the meal out on Fridays and the new phone I was going to get. I'd ask my mum whether there's more work at the bakery if the app gets worse. And I'd tell Tomasz to get his name down for the maintenance training at his place before the robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, then more than uneasy when I think about Tomasz. I don't like things changing that I can't control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell Tomasz to get on the maintenance training. Would he?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's stubborn, like me. But he listens to his dad, and his dad worked at the steelworks before it shut, so he knows what it's like. I think he'd do it if his dad told him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the app cut your pay a lot, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go back to my mum's bakery full time, even if it pays less. At least my mum doesn't change my wages with a text message. I'd rather earn less from family than more from a phone.

say: I'd say it's the **office people's problem**, not mine, because parcels still need hands.
I'd tell friends at church I **won't be using** any of it.
think: The **app's computer** will squeeze more parcels into the same hours.
My fiancé Tomasz's **warehouse** will get robots before my route does.
do: Stop the **Friday meals out** and the new phone.
Ask my mum about **more bakery hours** if the app gets worse.
Push Tomasz onto the **maintenance training** at his warehouse.
feel: **Uneasy** at first, then **worried** when I think about Tomasz's job.
S1.quote: I'd rather earn less from family than more from a phone.
fieldNote: She sees AI arriving **through the app**, not through anything she'd choose to use.
Her fiancé's **warehouse job** worries her more than her own route.
Falling back on her **mum's bakery** shows her trust in family over platforms.
Anxious: household income could shrink, but she still feels some control.

steps.text: Stop Friday meals out and skip the new phone
Ask her mum for more hours at the Church Street bakery
Get Tomasz onto the maintenance training at his warehouse

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before the wedding's paid off. And robots by 2031 doing the hands-on work as well, so my driving too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, that nobody voted for this, and that they should slow it down. I'd say it at the depot and at church, and maybe I'd even sign a petition, which I never do. People in my town want work, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm finished as a driver by about 2031, and Tomasz too, maybe sooner. The thinking part comes first, so the depot office goes, and then a few years later a robot van drives out to the reservoir. I don't have any other skill except baking bread and knowing where the farm dogs are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd sit down with Tomasz and work out the wedding, maybe make it smaller and earlier, at the church hall instead of the hotel, and keep the hotel money in the bank. I'd work every block I can get for the next two years to build savings. Then I'd talk to my mum about taking over the bakery one day, because people still want bread from a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Like being told the house is going to flood and you can only take what you can carry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we'd be fine because we've got each other and our families, even if I didn't fully believe it. Then probably I'd cry in the bathroom so he didn't see. He'd be pretending too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about learning any of the AI tools, even to help the bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds daft. I'd rather my mum and me did the orders on paper like always, and people can ring up. If that loses us customers, so be it.

say: I'd say **nobody voted** for this and they should slow it down.
I'd say people in my town want **work, not handouts**.
think: I'm probably **finished as a driver** by about 2031, and so is Tomasz.
My only other skill is **baking bread**, from my mum's shop.
do: Make the wedding **smaller and earlier** at the church hall and bank the hotel money.
Work **every block** I can get for two years.
Talk to my mum about **taking over** the bakery one day.
feel: **Frightened**, like being told the house will flood.
Putting on a **brave face** for Tomasz.
S2.quote: I don't have any other skill except baking bread and knowing where the farm dogs are.
fieldNote: She expects **both incomes** in the household to go within about five years.
Her refusal to touch **AI tools**, even for the bakery, is firm and knowing.
Her plan rests on **family**: the church hall wedding and her mum's bakery.
Alarmed: she expects to lose her job and is hiding fear from her fiancé.

steps.text: Move the wedding to the church hall and make it earlier
Work every parcel block possible and bank the hotel money
Ask her mum about taking over the bakery one day
Sign a petition asking the government to slow AI down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the computer thing, and then robots driving around 2034. That gives me longer, but it's the same in the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, that it's not right and somebody should stop it. Maybe I'd be a bit less loud, because 2034 sounds far off to most people. My nan would say you can't stop the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd tell myself I've got time and then do nothing for three years, because that's what I'm like. Then around 2031 the depot office would empty out, and I'd panic. I know that about myself, which is the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the wedding as planned next August, because there's time. I'd start working Saturdays at my mum's bakery instead of takeaways, to learn the ordering and the ovens properly. And I'd keep putting money aside, maybe 200 a month, for when the parcel work goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a dentist appointment that's far away. You forget it, but it's always there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably do nothing for three years. What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing Pete or someone at the depot lose their job. When it's a face you know, it's real. Until then it's just a story on the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Tomasz still try for children on the same timeline?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We want children soon after the wedding, and I wouldn't change that for a computer. But maybe we'd wait a year to see how Tomasz's job goes. Waiting on robots before my fiancé and I can plan a baby is the bit I'd hate most.

say: I'd still say it's **not right** and someone should stop it.
I'd be **a bit quieter**, since 2034 sounds far off to most people.
think: I'd likely **do nothing** for three years, then panic when the depot office empties.
Seeing **someone I know** lose their job is what would make it real.
do: Keep the **wedding next August** as planned.
Swap Saturday takeaways for **shifts at the bakery** to learn ordering and the ovens.
Save about **200 a month** for when parcel work goes.
feel: Like a **far-off dentist appointment**: forgotten, but always there.
S3.quote: Waiting on robots before my fiancé and I can plan a baby is the bit I'd hate most.
fieldNote: She is honest about **her own delay**, which is unusual and revealing.
The **baby timeline** is the most painful thing at stake for her.
Moving Saturdays to the **bakery** is her only skill-building step.
Still alarmed: she expects to lose her job, just later, with no plan beyond family.

steps.text: Keep the August wedding but wait a year before trying for children
Save about 200 a month for when parcel work goes
Work Saturdays at her mum's bakery instead of takeaway shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years for the computers, and robots around 2039. I'd be nearly 40 by then. That's a whole life away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no point worrying about 2039 when I've got a wedding to pay for. That's what everyone at the depot would say too. Maybe I'd say they'll find something else for us, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd believe it less. Ten years is a long time and they said self-driving cars were coming when I was at school. But if it's true, I'd rather be in the bakery by then, with our own regulars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep the wedding, kids, all of it as planned. Maybe in five years I'd go into the bakery with my mum properly. And I'd stay out of the AI stuff, because I don't need it for bread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm on the outside. A bit of a cold feeling when I think of being 40 with no job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it did come to that in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies and the people who make the phones, but also us, a bit, for letting it in. We used to buy bread from my mum, now people order everything to the door, and I deliver it. I'm part of it, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the government should do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want a handout. I'd want help for small family shops like ours to keep going, maybe lower business rates. Let people work, that's all.

say: I'd say there's **no point worrying** about 2039 with a wedding to pay for.
I'd say they'll **find something else** for us, they always do.
think: I half **don't believe it**, after the self-driving car promises at school.
If it's real, I'd rather be in **the bakery** with our own regulars.
do: Keep the **wedding and children** on the plans we have now.
Move into my mum's bakery properly **in about five years**.
feel: **Calm outside**, with a **cold feeling** about being 40 with no job.
S4.quote: We used to buy bread from my mum, now people order everything to the door, and I deliver it.
fieldNote: She **blames herself a little**, seeing her own deliveries as part of the shift.
She wants **lower business rates** for family shops, not handouts.
Ten years makes her **doubt** the change, which slows any action.
Anxious, not calm: she still expects to lose her driving work by 2039.

steps.text: Keep driving the village parcel route for now
Join her mum's bakery full time in about five years
Back lower business rates for small family shops

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it would take my work and Tomasz's before we've even had children. What would help is support for family businesses like my mum's bakery, so there's somewhere for people like me to go. And a real person at the parcel app you could actually ring.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my older customers. Half of the old people on my route only see a face because I bring a parcel, and a robot van won't knock on the window and wave. Somebody should think about them.

headlineQuote: Half of the old people on my route only see a face because I bring a parcel, and a robot van won't knock on the window and wave.
portrait: Carla is a **27-year-old parcel driver** covering villages past the reservoir in her own old hatchback.
She **never uses AI tools** and trusts family, church and her mum's bakery over apps.
She's engaged to Tomasz, a **warehouse forklift driver**, and their wedding is next August.
With **two years' warning** she's alarmed and shrinks the wedding to protect savings.
Even with ten years she expects to lose driving, and plans to **join the bakery**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it takes her job and her fiancé's before they have children.
whatWouldHelp: Support for **family businesses** like her mum's bakery.
A **real person** at the parcel app she can ring.
